paper_title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. In this work, we present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher OnPolicy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), fully open and complete recipe for post-training vision-language image models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: STEM, image perception, and video. We first curate two datasets across the three domains, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reason1 ing benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. To support reproducible research, we release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage. 1. Introduction Open recipes for reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced quickly: OpenMMReasoner [102], Video-R1 [13], Video-Thinker [69], OneThinker [14] and Vero [58] all report strong results on image or video benchmarks. Most of them follow two phases, which have been common since DeepSeek-R1 [22]. supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase, often on mix of domains (MixSFT), gives the model cold start and teaches it reasoning style, and reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards on mixeddomain prompts (MixRL) then strengthens its reasoning. Vero shows that MixRL alone, on large mixed set of 600K samples, also works without SFT, and recent VLM releases similarly train on the union of the domain data [5, 19]. Another route trains one RL expert per domain and then merges their weights [24, 85], and recent text studies often compare this route with MixRL [67, 79]. More recently, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has become better alternative to off-policy distillation [2, 20]. In OPD, the student samples its own responses and the teacher scores every token of the response, which reduces the exposure bias of training on teacher-generated text. Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) extends OPD to one RL teacher per domain, where each prompt goes to the teacher of its domain, and has become common post-training method to unify the capabilities of one model [45, 82, 92]. Building on this, several studies report that MOPD outperforms MixRL on text [45] and on images [37, 84], and also weight merging [45, 84]. They give two reasons: in MixRL, gain in one domain can come with loss in another [45], and the gradients of different capabilities conflict [84], whereas MOPD keeps the skill of each domain in dedicated teacher. However, this recipe is not yet well established for reasoning VLMs. MMVistaReason [37] also goes from SFT through GSPO experts to MOPD, but it covers images only. SCOPED [84] also distills image-skill experts only, and Video-MOPD [53] adds video teachers but compares only against model merging. These recipes end at distillation, and other multimodal students add the reward inside the distillation stage [35, 106]. Moreover, comparison of MOPD and MixRL as competing routes misses how the two relate. In the two-phase recipe, MixRL starts from the base or SFT model and has two tasks at once: it must merge the capabilities of all domains into one policy, and it must push the reasoning of that policy further. Since MOPD has proven more effective at the first of these tasks [37, 45], its student offers stronger starting point for RL than the base or SFT model. This raises question that the comparison leaves open: from this new starting point, can RL on the same data still carry the model further? To our knowledge, such separate rewarddriven stage after MOPD remains unstudied for VLMs. In this work, we present Multimodal Model MultiTeacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPDReasoner), fully open recipe for reasoning VLMs across image STEM reasoning (math, science, and logic probimage perception reasoning (charts, documents, lems), counting, and spatial questions), and video reasoning (Figure 2). We first build the data of each domain (Section 3.1), and on these data, starting from Qwen3.5-9B [54], we compare post-training recipes. The mixed-training recipes train one model on the union of the domain data with MixSFT, MixRL, or both. The multi-teacher recipe trains one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [107] on the RL prompts of that domain, directly or after an SFT warm-up, and then distills the three teachers into one student with MOPD. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe (Section 4.2). Finally, we initialize MixRL from the MOPD student and train it on the same prompts with the same GSPO settings. This additional stage further improves the student and yields our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. Beyond the final model, we release every part of the recipe, from the data and the training code to the checkpoints of all stages. Our contributions are as follows: We build fully open recipe for the three reasoning domains and release all of it: the data, with M3OPD-SFT1.35M (1.35M samples for SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K (193K prompts with verifiable answers for RL), the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage. We compare post-training recipes for multimodal reasoning on the same data, from mixed training with MixSFT and MixRL to MOPD of GSPO domain teachers with or without an SFT warm-up, and we establish MOPD of teachers trained directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: its student matches each teacher on its own domain and is above the mixed-training baselines overall. We study MixRL on top of the MOPD student as final stage, which starts RL from the stronger point that MOPD provides instead of from the base model. To our knowledge, this is the first study of separate RL stage after multi-teacher distillation in VLMs. On the same prompts and settings, the stage still improves the MOPD student with no collapse, and we analyze how the stronger start changes the course of MixRL. 2. Related work On-policy and multi-teacher distillation. On-policy distillation [2, 20] is now standard post-training stage for small models [86]. For VLMs, single-teacher variants reweight visually grounded tokens [38], steer the update toward visual grounding [95], or transfer reasoning from text teacher [7]. Open RL recipes for reasoning. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards drives recent gains in LLM reasoning, with group-based methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [22, 59] and the sequence-level GSPO [107]. Open VLM recipes apply these methods to image reasoning [30, 47, 58, 66, 102], to video understanding [13, 32, 68], and to both in one model [14]. We use perdomain GSPO only to build the teachers, and we use MixRL both as baseline and as new final stage on top of the distilled student. few text recipes also continue with RL after MOPD: Nemotron-Cascade 2 runs further domain RL stages [92], and iterated MOPD retrains per-domain teachers from the student [45]. For single-teacher text OPD, the distilled model is also stronger start for later RL than the SFT model [1]. For omni-modal and GUI students, OPOD and UI-MOPD instead optimize reward inside the distillation stage [35, 106], and the multi-teacher VLM recipes above end at MOPD. Recipe We present our recipe, which consolidates three domain teachers into one vision-language model by Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), over three reasoning doimage STEM, image perception, and video. All mains: models build on Qwen3.5-9B [54], and, as shown in Figure 2, the recipe has three stages: (1) domain teachers, each trained with GSPO, (2) MOPD of the three teachers into one student, and (3) MixRL on top of the MOPD student. 3.1. Data Domains and sources. Each domain has an SFT set and an RL prompt set, built from public datasets. We show every source with its size in Figure 3 and provide more details in Appendix A. Image STEM covers math, science, and visual logic problems, mainly from MMFineReason [36], MMVistaReason [37], DeepVision-103K [62], the STEM part of Vero [58], and ViRL39K [66]. Image perception covers charts, documents, OCR, counting, grounding, and spatial questions, mainly from FineVision [76], ChartVerse [41], ChartNet [26], and the perception parts of Vero. Finally, video comes mainly from VideoChat3 [33], LLaVA-Video-178K [104], OneThinker [14], LongVideoReason [10], Video-HopChain [49], CapRL-VideoQA [88], and TimeLens [100, 108]. SFT traces. The SFT sets serve the MixSFT baseline and the SFT warm-up of the teachers that we compare (Section 3.3). We replace each response of the SFT sources with new sample from model that we give the gold final answer. This model, the generator, receives the media, the question, and the gold answer, and it writes thinking trace and reply that ends in that answer. After generation, we drop trace if its final answer differs from the gold answer, if it refers to the given answer, if the generator rejects the gold, or if it is truncated or degenerate. Choice of the trace generator. For each domain, we consider two generators: Qwen3.5-9B itself, which gives self traces, and the larger and stronger Qwen3.8-FlashNext [56]. stronger generator can write better traces, but work on OPD shows that stronger teacher is not always better one, because the gain depends on the compatibility between the student and the teacher [1, 34, 45]. Self traces, in contrast, stay close to the response distribution of Qwen3.5-9B, so SFT on them changes the reasoning style of the model less before the later stages. We therefore train one SFT model of each domain on each trace source and compare the two  (Table 1)  . On both image domains, self traces give the better model, with clear margin on image STEM, whereas on video, self traces give slightly worse model than the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next traces. We thus use self traces for image STEM and image perception and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next traces for video. The final SFT set, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M, has 1.35M samples: the 994K image self traces (368K for image STEM and 626K for image perception) and one Qwen3.8-Flash-Next trace for each of the 357K video questions. RL prompts. The RL sets keep only prompts with ruleverifiable answer: 64,307 for image STEM, 67,915 for image perception and 60,805 for video. The union of the three sets (193,027 prompts) forms M3OPD-RL-193K, the prompt set of MOPD and MixRL, where each prompt keeps its domain label. Prompt template. All stages use the native Qwen3.5 chat template with thinking enabled and no system prompt. The user turn holds the media and the question, followed by one format line for the answer type, e.g. Put your final answer within boxed{}. for math. We also remove the answerformat instructions of the source questions, so each prompt has exactly one format instruction. Deduplication and decontamination. In the SFT question pool, we remove samples with near-identical media and the same normalized question across all domains. We then decontaminate all SFT and RL sets against the evaluation benchmarks of Section 4.1. We remove sample if it contains at least half of the word 13-grams of benchmark question, if one of its images is within perceptualhash (pHash) distance of 4 of benchmark image, or if its video shares source video identifier or frame hash with benchmark video. Finally, the SFT and RL sets are disjoint on the prompt and media hash. 3.2. We initialize the student from Qwen3.5-9B, the model that all teachers come from, and we run MOPD once for each set of three teachers. 3.5. MixRL on top of MOPD In the common recipe, the RL prompts serve single stage, MixRL from the base or SFT model, which has to merge the capabilities of all domains into one policy and to strengthen its reasoning at the same time. These two roles compete: MixRL can harm individual capabilities [37, 84], and the MixSFT model has mainly learned reasoning style, so it must learn all domains from sparse reward at once while it also sharpens its reasoning. In our recipe, MOPD assumes the first role: distillation merges the capabilities of all three teachers into one policy and already matches or outperforms the MixRL baseline (Section 4.2). The MOPD student is therefore stronger starting point for RL than the model from which MixRL usually starts. At the same time, MOPD trains the student to match its teachers, so the teachers bound what the distillation loss can teach, whereas reward-driven stage does not depend on any teacher and can move the student past this bound. We therefore use the prompts once more, with MixRL on top of the MOPD student, to examine whether RL from this starting point further improves the model on the same data. With the teachers trained directly from Qwen3.5-9B, the result is our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup Models. We use Qwen3.5-9B [54] as the base model of every run, and we train SFT with lmms-engine [42] and GSPO and MOPD with verl [61], with vLLM [29] for the rollout. Appendix gives all training settings. Benchmarks. We evaluate on 21 benchmarks in three domains, and for image STEM reasoning, we use DynaMath [109], EMMA [23], LogicVista [81], MathVerse [103], MathVista [44], MMMU [96], MMMUPro [97] and We-Math [52]. For image perception reasoning, we use AI2D [25], CountBenchQA [6, 51], CVBench [65], HallusionBench [21], MMStar [8], OCRBench [40], RealWorldQA [80] and SimpleVQA [12]. For video reasoning, we use LongVideoBench [77], TempCompass [39], Video-Holmes [11], Video-MME [15] and VSIBench [87]. In addition, all training data is decontaminated against these benchmarks (Section 3.1). Evaluation. We evaluate all models with one protocol in lmms-eval [101], with thinking enabled and cap of 32768 tokens per response, thinking included. We sample eight responses per question (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20) and report the mean accuracy over the eight samples (avg@8). Images are resized to at most 1,605,632 pixels, and each video frame has at most 65,536 pixels. Videos shorter than 150 seconds are sampled at 1 fps with at least 4 frames, and from longer videos we sample 150 evenly spaced frames. Appendix gives the dataset, split and metric of each benchmark and the judge of SimpleVQA. Compared models. We compare two families of recipes on the same data. The mixed-training recipes train one model on all domains with no teachers: MixSFT trains Qwen3.5-9B on the union of the three domain SFT sets (Section 3.1), the MixRL baseline runs GSPO from the MixSFT checkpoint on the same prompt union as MOPD, with the same GSPO settings as the domain teachers, and we also run the same MixRL directly from Qwen3.5-9B. The multi-teacher recipes distill one set of domain teachers into one student with MOPD, where the teachers are trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B or after an SFT warm-up. For each set of teachers, MixRL on top of MOPD uses the same prompts and the same GSPO settings as the MixRL baseline (Section 3.5). The SFT warm-ups and the domain teachers are three models each, one per domain, and we evaluate each of them only on the benchmarks of its own domain, whereas we evaluate all other models on all 21 benchmarks. 4.2. In both mixed-training runs, Training dynamics. the training accuracy rises during the run and the response length changes strongly, upward from MixSFT and downward from Qwen3.5-9B. In contrast, both MOPD students start MixRL with training accuracy that these runs only approach at the end of the shown steps, and change this length much less (Figure 6(a) and (c)). Much of both mixedtraining runs thus builds skills that the domain teachers have and that MOPD already transfers to the student. The group filter drops prompt when all of its responses are correct or all are wrong, because such group gives no advantage signal. From the first step, both students solve more than half of the sampled prompts in all eight responses and start with fewer prompts with no correct response than the mixed-training runs (Figure 6(b)), so the prompts that remain after the filter give their learning signal at higher level of ability. The entropy of the policy also differs (Figure 6(d)): MixRL from MixSFT starts with low entropy, whereas the other three runs start with higher entropy and keep it above this run, and no run shows sign of entropy collapse. Since RL mainly sharpens behavior that its start model already shows [17, 98], the start of MixRL decides how far the same prompts can carry the model. Measures. We study the reasoning of the models at the level of their outputs and treat the thinking part of response as sequence of reasoning moves. We derive the moves from the responses: we collect the most frequent sentence openings in the responses of all models, group them into moves, and check each group by reading samples of the matched sentences. Similar to the cognitive behaviors of Gandhi et al. [17], we count three moves of self-monitoring, namely verifying result (e.g. lets double-check, this matches), revising step (e.g. wait, let me reconsider), and considering an alternative (e.g. or maybe, lets assume), which we call self-checks. Since our models express the same move either in the native style of Qwen3.59B (Lets check) or in the first-person style of our SFT traces (Let me check, need to), each move covers both phrasings, and we normalize the count by the thinking length. We further describe the allocation of the thinking budget as the ratio of the thinking length on hard questions to that on easy questions, where we rank the questions by the mean solve rate of five models (the domain teachers trained directly from Qwen3.5-9B, their MOPD student, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B, MixSFT and the MixRL baseline, with easy questions at solve rate of at least 0.9 and hard questions at most 0.25), the stability as the share of responses with at least five repeated lines, the decisiveness as the share of responses that hedge (e.g. probably, Ill go with), and, on video, the grounding as the number of cited timestamps. Conclusion We presented M3OPD-Reasoner, fully open recipe for reasoning VLMs over image STEM, image perception and video. On the same curated data, MOPD of GSPO teachers trained directly from Qwen3.5-9B is the best of the compared recipes, and with or without the SFT warmup, MOPD and MixRL complement each other, as MOPD merges the domain teachers into stronger starting point for RL than the base model, and MixRL still improves this student on the same data with no collapse. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.

Data A.1. Sources Each domain has an SFT set and an RL prompt set built from public datasets  (Table 7)  . For the SFT sets, we keep the questions and gold answers of the sources and replace the original responses with samples from model that we give the gold final answer. The SFT question pool contains only single-turn questions with at least one image or video, and multi-turn sources keep their last question. In contrast, the RL sets keep only prompts with rule-verifiable answers, and Table 8 gives their answer types. Within one source, stable hash of the image, video or question splits the items between SFT, RL and held-out pool, and the SFT part of source excludes the images of its RL part. Finally, several RL sources are subsampled, and the pass-rate filters of DeepVision-103K and ViRL39K keep the harder items. Table 7. Data sources and sizes after deduplication and decontamination. SFT is the SFT set of the domain, which serves the SFT warm-up of the domain teacher that we compare and is part of the MixSFT set, and RL the RL prompt set of the domain teacher.
